summary:
Elemental sulfur is how you lower soil pH without adding salt: soil bacteria oxidise it to sulfuric acid, which acidifies the soil over several months. It returns pH change, elemental sulfur, sulfur per 100 m² and sulfur per 1 000 ft², and the panel shows all of them at once.

The amount depends on how far the pH has to fall and on the texture — a sand needs a third of what a clay needs for the same change. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Sulfur Soil Acidifier
sections.html:
Sulfur (kg) ≈ area (m²) × ΔpH × texture factor × 0.2. One pH unit on a loam takes about 20 kg per 100 m² (≈ 4 lb per 100 ft²)

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
ΔpHhow many pH units you need to come down—
S⁰elemental sulfur, oxidised by soil bacteria to sulfuric acid—
texture factor0.5 for sand, 1 for loam, 1.5 for clay — clay buffers more—

sections.title: How do I use the Sulfur Soil Acidifier?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the area and the pH from your soil test, plus the pH you want.
  2. Choose the texture; clay needs the most sulfur, sand the least.
  3. The sulfur to apply is given in kilograms and in pounds per 1 000 ft², with the months it will take.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: area of 100 m², current ph of 7.5 pH, target ph of 6.5 pH, soil texture set to 1.0.

Substituting them into the formula gives ph change of 1 units, elemental sulfur of 20 kg, sulfur per 100 m² of 20 kg, sulfur per 1 000 ft² of 2 lb, time to take effect of 3 months.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
under 0.5 unitTrim0.5–1 kg per 10 m² on a loam
0.5 – 1 unitTypicalapply in autumn so winter rain works it in
over 1.5 unitsLarge changesplit over two years and retest between

  • Sulfur is slow: the bacteria need warm, moist, aerated soil and it can take six months to a year. For a fast change use aluminium sulfate or a pH-adjusted mix, at the cost of adding salts.

  • Never change pH by more than about one unit in a single season — the shift is uneven and the plants in the patch get shocked.

  • Sulfur does not move far in soil. Incorporate it into the root zone rather than spreading it on the surface.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Expecting a pH change within a week — elemental sulfur needs microbial oxidation.
  • Using lime to raise pH and sulfur to lower it on the same bed in one season.
  • Applying sulfur to dry soil in a cold month, where the bacteria do nothing at all.

faq.q: How long does elemental sulfur take to lower pH?
faq.a: Three to twelve months, depending on temperature, moisture and how finely ground it is.

faq.q: How much sulfur to lower pH by one unit?
faq.a: About 20 kg per 100 m² on a loam, roughly half that on sand and one and a half times on clay.
It acts within weeks, but adds aluminium and salt; sulfur is gentler and slower.

faq.q: What does the Sulfur Soil Acidifier actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns pH change, elemental sulfur, sulfur per 100 m² and sulfur per 1 000 ft². Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
